title: AliExpress Category Tariff Splitter
oneLiner: A hobbyist import cart tool that predicts per-category customs fees before a cheap order becomes an expensive bundle.
targetUser: 3D printing hobbyists, electronics tinkerers, cosplay makers, and micro-import buyers building mixed-category carts.
keyUX: Paste a cart, tag categories, drag items between shipment groups, compare category-fee scenarios, and export a split-or-ship recommendation.
sourceSignals: S8 - Reddit r/3DDruck tariff/category fee anxiety: https://www.reddit.com/r/3DDruck/comments/1smvhzk/sind_die_im_juni_kommenden_aliexpress_z%C3%B6lle_f%C3%BCr/?tl=en
stitchPrompt: Create a responsive web app called "AliExpress Category Tariff Splitter" for 3D printing hobbyists, electronics tinkerers, cosplay makers, and micro-import buyers building mixed-category carts. The app is based on observed user pull: hobbyists already read tariff summaries, ask communities whether category fees stack, split orders by gut feel, and delay cheap parts purchases when customs math is unclear. The app should use a cart splitter mechanic around the trigger moment "a mixed-category import cart looks cheap before checkout" and make the first screen communicate "Your cheap cart is hiding category fees." Use the user's own language: "Should I split this order before the category fees stack?" Build the core workflow around item names, category tags, item prices, shipment grouping, country rule, shipping delay, and fee assumptions, and produce a split-or-ship recommendation card. Required sections: cheap-cart warning header, item/category tagging table, drag-to-split shipment canvas, fee scenario comparison, rule explanation drawer, delivery delay tradeoff strip, household budget impact card, and shareable split-or-ship verdict. Emotional pressure to make visible: 자산 방어, surprise customs fees, hobby delay, and embarrassment about a supposedly cheap order. Design direction: use the `financial-analyst` profile with clean off-white comparison panels, graphite item rows, muted green savings deltas, amber uncertainty bands, stable drag/drop cards, and no generic ecommerce hero. Avoid generic dashboard framing; make the main interaction feel like physically splitting a cart and watching fees change.
